text.text: Despite age being a significant sociodemographic correlate of conspiratorial mentality, surprisingly little is known about its precursors and consequences among older people.
Older people are often considered at risk of psychological distress, which often relates to conspiratorial mentality.
Our study therefore assumed bidirectional relations between these constructs.
Distress was represented by loneliness, anxiety, and depression.
We also investigated potential moderation by social media use, as conspiracy theories tend to be disseminated on such media.
We tested these associations linearly and quadratically using data from a two-wave longitudinal study of Czech adults aged 60+ (NW1 = 4133, MageW1 = 69.1).
Conspiratorial mentality was not predicted by other variables, indicating that these are probably not risk factors for such mentality.
Conversely, conspiratorial mentality positively predicted only anxiety.
Social media use moderation and quadratic effects were unsupported.
Overall, the study suggests that conspiratorial mentality can be an anxiety-provoking experience among older people.

Conspiracy theories allege that two or more powerful individuals (or groups) have secretly colluded to bring about a nefarious outcome to benefit themselves and harm the common good (Biddlestone et al., 2025; Bowes et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Conspiracy theories allege that two or more powerful individuals (or groups) have secretly colluded to bring about a nefarious outcome to benefit themselves and harm the common good <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Biddlestone et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bowes et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Belief in such theories is considered widespread in the contemporary interconnected world and has the potential to infiltrate public discourse.

These beliefs are also associated with outcomes that are harmful to our society, such as undermining democracy (e.g., Albertson & Guiler, 2020; Mari et al., 2022) or motivating political violence (Rousis et al., 2022; Vegetti & Littvay, 2022).
text.formatted: These beliefs are also associated with outcomes that are harmful to our society, such as undermining democracy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Albertson & Guiler, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Mari et al., 2022)</ref> or motivating political violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Rousis et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Vegetti & Littvay, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Given that conspiracy theories are widespread on the internet, it is no surprise that social media use is considered a risk factor for conspiratorial mentality (Pilch et al., 2023), despite its impact not reaching the commonly feared potential (Douglas et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Given that conspiracy theories are widespread on the internet, it is no surprise that social media use is considered a risk factor for conspiratorial mentality <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Pilch et al., 2023)</ref>, despite its impact not reaching the commonly feared potential <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Douglas et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The potential harm is not only at the societal level, but negative consequences can also occur for the individual.

Belief in conspiracy theories is often associated with worse individual well-being or mental health (Bowes et al., 2023; Flaskerud, 2021; Pilch et al., 2023; Zwar et al., 2022), although robust directionality is not yet established.
text.formatted: Belief in conspiracy theories is often associated with worse individual well-being or mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bowes et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Flaskerud, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Pilch et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Zwar et al., 2022)</ref>, although robust directionality is not yet established.

text.text: Explanations in the existing literature suggest that conspiracy theories are especially attractive to people seeking to satisfy basic unmet psychological needs, specifically those rooted in epistemic, existential, and social motives (Biddlestone et al., 2025; Douglas et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Explanations in the existing literature suggest that conspiracy theories are especially attractive to people seeking to satisfy basic unmet psychological needs, specifically those rooted in epistemic, existential, and social motives <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Biddlestone et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Douglas et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Respectively, people believe in conspiracies to find comprehensive explanations for complex phenomena, to understand uncontrollable existential threats and regain a sense of autonomy over them, and to maintain and defend the image of oneself and the groups to which one belongs.
However, conspiratorial mentality may be more appealing than satisfying as it does not necessarily fulfil these motives in a healthy way (Liekefett et al., 2021; van Prooijen, 2019).
text.formatted: However, conspiratorial mentality may be more appealing than satisfying as it does not necessarily fulfil these motives in a healthy way <ref type="bibr">(Liekefett et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">van Prooijen, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: That is, conspiratorial mentality can lead to psychological distress that was formerly tried to cope with.

This might be one of the reasons that belief in conspiracies is often associated with symptoms of psychological ill-being, such as anxiety (Bowes et al., 2023; Pilch et al., 2023), loneliness (Biddlestone et al., 2025; Bierwiaczonek et al., 2024) or depression (Pilch et al., 2023; Zwar et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This might be one of the reasons that belief in conspiracies is often associated with symptoms of psychological ill-being, such as anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bowes et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Pilch et al., 2023)</ref>, loneliness <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Biddlestone et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bierwiaczonek et al., 2024)</ref> or depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Pilch et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Zwar et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Although this motivational mechanism received general support, evidence on more specific age cohorts is scarcer.
This is surprising because age is considered one of the most important sociodemographic correlates of conspiratorial mentality (Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2025).
text.formatted: This is surprising because age is considered one of the most important sociodemographic correlates of conspiratorial mentality <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present paper focuses on conspiratorial mentality among the older population.

Although existing research suggests that young people tend to believe in conspiracy theories more than older people (Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2025; Enders et al., 2024; Klofstad et al., 2019), this does not imply that older people are without any risks.
text.formatted: Although existing research suggests that young people tend to believe in conspiracy theories more than older people <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Enders et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Klofstad et al., 2019)</ref>, this does not imply that older people are without any risks.

text.text: Specifically, older people are more likely to disseminate false information online (Brashier & Schacter, 2020; Guess et al., 2019; Ramos & Van Boven, 2026) and can turn to potentially conspiratorial online communities to deal with unpleasant experiences to which older adults are more at risk, such as social isolation (Meini & Rosola, 2025), friendship breakdowns (Vivion et al., 2024), or anxiety (Jafarnezhad Dehmiani et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Specifically, older people are more likely to disseminate false information online <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brashier & Schacter, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Guess et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Ramos & Van Boven, 2026)</ref> and can turn to potentially conspiratorial online communities to deal with unpleasant experiences to which older adults are more at risk, such as social isolation <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Meini & Rosola, 2025)</ref>, friendship breakdowns <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Vivion et al., 2024)</ref>, or anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Jafarnezhad Dehmiani et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, although generally having lower levels of conspiratorial mentality, older adults might still be more susceptible to believing specific conspiracy theories (Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2025), such as those related to health (e.g., about vaccines; Enders & Smallpage, 2019; Klofstad et al., 2019).

text.text: In this paper, we aim to expand this line of research and focus on the older population.

Although they are much less studied, this age group can still be at risk, especially of relational breakdowns, which might foster their susceptibility to conspiracy theories and their dissemination online.
Specifically, we want to longitudinally investigate the association between conspiratorial mentality and selected factors of psychological distress (i.e., loneliness, anxiety, and depression).
Given that people can encounter conspiracy theories on social media, where these theories are often disseminated (Douglas et al., 2019), we also consider the role of social media use.
text.formatted: Given that people can encounter conspiracy theories on social media, where these theories are often disseminated <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Douglas et al., 2019)</ref>, we also consider the role of social media use.

text.text: Although older age is associated with a lower tendency to conspiratorial mentality (Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2025; Enders et al., 2024; Klofstad et al., 2019), some inconsistencies exist in the literature.
text.formatted: Although older age is associated with a lower tendency to conspiratorial mentality <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Enders et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Klofstad et al., 2019)</ref>, some inconsistencies exist in the literature.

text.text: Specifically, some studies found that older people were more likely to be exposed to and share conspiracy theories on social media (Brashier & Schacter, 2020; Grinberg et al., 2019; Guess et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Specifically, some studies found that older people were more likely to be exposed to and share conspiracy theories on social media <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brashier & Schacter, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Grinberg et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Guess et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Studies have proposed several explanations for this finding, typically referring to the decreased ability to discriminate between false and accurate information among older people (e.g., Guess et al., 2019; Peng et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Studies have proposed several explanations for this finding, typically referring to the decreased ability to discriminate between false and accurate information among older people (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Guess et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Peng et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, such an approach can be overly simplistic and potentially harmful due to neglecting the experiences of older people.
For example, older people tend to have more fragile social networks and are thus at risk of loneliness or social isolation (Vivion et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, older people tend to have more fragile social networks and are thus at risk of loneliness or social isolation <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Vivion et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Other authors link these experiences to internet use, as older people often have lower digital literacy when dealing with online news media.

Combined with interpersonal trust, which tends to be higher among older people, this can also potentially foster their susceptibility to conspiracy theories, especially when shared by familiar people online (Brashier & Schacter, 2020).
text.formatted: Combined with interpersonal trust, which tends to be higher among older people, this can also potentially foster their susceptibility to conspiracy theories, especially when shared by familiar people online <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brashier & Schacter, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Several characteristics of older adults may also increase their vulnerability to conspiratorial mentality.
Older people can experience increased stress, anxiety, or worries when encountering online (mis)information and when experiencing information overload (Vivion et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Older people can experience increased stress, anxiety, or worries when encountering online (mis)information and when experiencing information overload <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Vivion et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, Meini and Rosola (2025) argue that older people might be more susceptible to false information online not only due to epistemic distress (i.e., the need for coherent information) but also due to social isolation and loneliness.
text.formatted: Moreover, <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Meini and Rosola (2025)</ref> argue that older people might be more susceptible to false information online not only due to epistemic distress (i.e., the need for coherent information) but also due to social isolation and loneliness.

text.text: In other words, seeking reinforcement of social identity and a sense of belonging can lead one to fall easily into online "epistemic bubbles" (Meini & Rosola, 2025), which may also be associated with exposure to conspiracy theories.
text.formatted: In other words, seeking reinforcement of social identity and a sense of belonging can lead one to fall easily into online "epistemic bubbles" <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Meini & Rosola, 2025)</ref>, which may also be associated with exposure to conspiracy theories.

text.text: Furthermore, loneliness is generally considered a risk for older people (e.g., Nyqvist et al., 2021; Xing et al., 2020), and it is also associated with psychological ill-being (Dahlberg et al., 2021; Fernandez-Rodrigues et al., 2022; Hubbard et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Furthermore, loneliness is generally considered a risk for older people (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Nyqvist et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Xing et al., 2020)</ref>, and it is also associated with psychological ill-being <ref type="bibr">(Dahlberg et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fernandez-Rodrigues et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hubbard et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the relationship may also operate in the opposite direction.

That is, unmet psychological needs may not only contribute to higher levels of conspiratorial mentality, but conspiratorial mentality itself may further increase psychological distress because it ultimately fails to satisfy those needs.
For example, people might turn to conspiracy theories for epistemic certainty and to alleviate anxiety associated with uncertainty.

However, given that conspiracies are inherently uncertain, they can be anxiety-provoking and promote the psychological distress that they were originally trying to mitigate (Bowes et al., 2023; Liekefett et al., 2023; van Prooijen, 2019).
text.formatted: However, given that conspiracies are inherently uncertain, they can be anxiety-provoking and promote the psychological distress that they were originally trying to mitigate <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bowes et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Liekefett et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">van Prooijen, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, it is essential to consider the role of social media, where conspiracy theories are often disseminated, and older people can engage with them.

Social media use might also explain differences in conspiratorial mentality across age cohorts, as young people are more engaged with new technologies and social media (e.g., Deckman, 2024) and are potentially more exposed to conspiracy theories.
text.formatted: Social media use might also explain differences in conspiratorial mentality across age cohorts, as young people are more engaged with new technologies and social media (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Deckman, 2024)</ref> and are potentially more exposed to conspiracy theories.

text.text: This exposure, either intentional or accidental, makes social media use a potential risk factor for conspiratorial mentality (Pilch et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This exposure, either intentional or accidental, makes social media use a potential risk factor for conspiratorial mentality <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Pilch et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, older people may be less likely to think conspiratorially because they tend to be less active on social media, and higher social media use might be linked to stronger conspiratorial mentality among them.

In this study, we focus on conspiratorial mentality (i.e., the general belief that conspiracies are happening) among older people, who, despite being generally less prone to such mentality, are not without risks.
We focus on three factors of psychological distress associated with belief in conspiracy theories: anxiety, loneliness, and depressive symptoms.

Based on existing literature, these factors can serve either as predictors (i.e., conspiratorial mentality seen as "coping" against these experiences or as an attempt to satisfy unmet needs underlying them) or as outcomes (i.e., conspiratorial mentality being an unsatisfying attempt to satisfy unmet psychological needs).
Thus, we assume bidirectional associations and employ a twowave longitudinal survey to establish the direction of these relationships.

Additionally, existing literature suggests that social media use may be a risk factor for conspiratorial mentality, as conspiracy theories are widespread on such platforms and people often engage with them (e.g., by reading or sharing them).

Thus, we assume that psychological factors, on their own, might not necessarily be associated with the adoption of a conspiratorial mentality among older people, but that this association is more pronounced among those who are more active on social media.
This is because people seeking to mitigate unpleasant psychological experiences may engage in conspiratorial mentality more when they are also more exposed to conspiracy theories online.
Based on the reasoning above, we proposed the following hypotheses: H1.
Anxiety, loneliness, and depressive symptoms will positively predict conspiratorial mentality.
Conspiratorial mentality will positively predict anxiety, loneliness, and depressive symptoms.
Social media use will positively predict conspiratorial mentality.
Anxiety, loneliness, and depressive symptoms will positively predict conspiratorial mentality more strongly with higher social media use.
Additionally, we also explore the possibility that at least some of the proposed effects are nonlinear rather than linear.
Specifically, it is possible that only markedly higher levels of conspiratorial mentality predict psychological distress.

For example, low or mild levels of conspiratorial mentality might represent healthy epistemic scepticism that does not necessarily cause further distress, but only high levels can become more disturbing.
This aligns with the fact that belief in conspiracies can be anxietyprovoking, which might be especially pronounced for people with strong conspiratorial beliefs.
Thus, we also investigate the quadratic effects of the hypothesised associations to explore this possibility of nonlinearity.
Including quadratic effects is also beneficial when testing interactions for detecting potentially spurious moderating effects (e.g., Belzak & Bauer, 2019; MacCallum & Mar, 1995).
text.formatted: Including quadratic effects is also beneficial when testing interactions for detecting potentially spurious moderating effects (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Belzak & Bauer, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">MacCallum & Mar, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Because existing literature overwhelmingly tests only linear effects, this part is exploratory.
Also, given that this work is based on secondary analyses, it was not preregistered.
This study uses two-wave longitudinal data on Czech older adults with a time lag of approximately twelve months.
The data were collected as part of a larger project (blinded for review).
As this project is still ongoing at the time of writing this work, data will be publicly available after the end of the project in 2029.
Participants were recruited via a professional agency and were compensated in accordance with the agency's rules.
Informed consent was obtained at the beginning of the questionnaire, and participants could withdraw from the study at any time during data collection.
Ethical approval for the study was obtained by the (blinded for review).

In Wave 1, 1323 (32.0%) participants had completed higher education (i.e., undergraduate, postgraduate), and 2810 (68.0%) had secondary or lower education.

Conspiratorial mentality was measured by the Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire (Bruder et al., 2013).

text.text: The scale consisted of five items (e.g., "Government agencies closely monitor all citizens") rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 -Completely disagree to 5 -Completely agree).

Due to the high residual correlations between two of the items (i.e., r > .10), we decided to drop one of the problematic items with the lowest factor loading ("Politicians usually do not tell us the true motives for their decisions"; λW1 = .62, λW2 = .51) from the model.

text.text: The final scale demonstrated an internal consistency of McDonald's ω = .86 in Wave 1 and McDonald's ω = .85 in Wave 2.
Loneliness was measured by the three-item version of the UCLA loneliness scale (Hughes et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Loneliness was measured by the three-item version of the UCLA loneliness scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hughes et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The items (e.g., "I feel left out") were rated on a four-point frequency scale (1 -Never to 4 -Often).
The scale demonstrated an internal consistency of McDonald's ω = .82 in Wave 1 and McDonald's ω = .85 in Wave 2.
Depression and anxiety were measured by the Czech version of the DASS-21 (Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995; Vilimovský & Kučera, 2018) questionnaire.

text.text: Depression was measured with seven items (e.g., "I felt as if I was unable to experience any pleasant feelings") and anxiety was measured by six items (e.g., "I felt dry in my mouth.").
Both scales used a four-point frequency response scale (1 -Didn't apply at all to 4 -It applied almost all the time).

Both scales demonstrated an internal consistency of McDonald's ω = .92 for depression and McDonald's ω = .87 for anxiety in Wave 1, and McDonald's ω = .94 for depression and McDonald's ω = .85 for anxiety in Wave 2.
Social media use was measured by one item, "How often do you do these activities? -Using social media".
The item used a five-point frequency response scale (1 -At least once a day to 5 -Not at all in the past year).
The responses were reversecoded for the analyses so that higher values represent higher social media use.
Wordings of all items are provided in Online Supplementary Material 1.
Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the unidimensionality and at least longitudinal metric measurement invariance of all included scales.
Factor loadings and the results of the measurement invariance tests are provided in Online Supplementary Material 2.
The hypotheses were tested in lavaan 0.7-3 (Rosseel, 2012) through a CLPM (for a conceptual diagram, see Figure 1).

text.text: Conspiratorial mentality, loneliness, anxiety, and depression were specified as latent factors with multiple indicators.
The number of indicators for anxiety and depression was lowered to three through parcelling by using an item-to-construct technique (Little et al., 2002).
text.formatted: The number of indicators for anxiety and depression was lowered to three through parcelling by using an item-to-construct technique <ref type="bibr">(Little et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Because the response scale for loneliness represented frequencies in ordered categories, we specified indicators for this scale as ordered categorical by the ordered command in lavaan and used the WLSMV estimator.
We also included age, gender, and education as time-invariant confounders for "control variables" purposes.
Missing data were handled by pairwise deletion.
The analysis consisted of two major steps.
First, we tested H1-H3 using the twowave CLPM, which included only the main effects.
Second, H4 was tested by extending the model to include interaction terms between social media use and loneliness, anxiety, and depression.
The interactions were analysed using the modsem package (v.1.0.16; Slupphaug et al., 2025), creating the interaction terms via the product indicator approach with double mean centering.
Finally, we conducted exploratory analyses by including quadratic terms in the modsem model.

Because models with latent interaction variables tend to produce incorrect estimates of model fit, we treated the fit indices of the first model (with main effects only) as a lower bound for the model with interaction terms, as suggested by Schoeman and Jorgensen (2021).

text.text: Overall, we find no support for H1 and H3, as conspiratorial mentality was not predicted by any of the included predictors (β = .005, p = .855, 95%CI [-.048;.057] for loneliness; β = .023, p = .581, 95%CI [-.060;.106] for depression; β = .039, p = .326, 95%CI [-.039;.117] for anxiety; β = -.003, p = .863, 95%CI [-.036;.030] for social media use).
We find some support for H2, as anxiety was positively predicted by conspiratorial mentality with a small-to-medium effect size (β = .053, p = .005, 95%CI [.016;.089]).
Apart from that, there were several significant temporal relations between loneliness, depression, and anxiety.
Social media use had no significant temporal association with other variables.
Also, given the significant autoregressive effects, all variables can be considered relatively stable.
For the full results, see Supplementary Materials 4.
The interaction model converged without issues.
However, interaction effects were overall non-significant (with βs ranging from -.029 to .055), and thus H4 was not supported.
As a result, we tested the quadratic model without these interaction terms.

Because the model with all quadratic effects yielded improper solutions (i.e., standardised coefficients exceeding 1), we tested the quadratic effects of loneliness, depression, and anxiety separately from the quadratic effects of conspiratorial mentality.

Overall, three of the quadratic effects were statistically significant: the effects of anxiety (β = .079, p = .011, 95%CI [.019;.139]) and social media use (β = -.066, p = .001, 95%CI [-.106;-.025]) on conspiratorial mentality, and the effect of conspiratorial mentality on loneliness (β = -.071, p = .003, 95%CI [-.117;-.025]).
See Figures 3, 4, and 5 for plots of these effects.

This work examined the longitudinal relationships between conspiratorial mentality and several indicators of psychological distress and social media use among older people.
Overall, the results did not support the hypotheses that our indicators of psychological distress predict conspiratorial mentality.

Although exploratory results on quadratic effects showed few significant results, those explained only a marginal amount of variance and thus will not be interpreted further to avoid overinterpretation.
On the other hand, conspiratorial mentality positively predicted subsequent anxiety, suggesting that such a mentality style is more distress-provoking than satisfying among older people.
Social media use did not moderate any of the hypothesised associations, suggesting that it might not be such a risk factor for conspiratorial mentality among older people.
Our main linear results provided no support for H1, suggesting that older people probably do not engage in conspiratorial mentality to cope with their psychological distress.

One potential explanation is that older people are more ingrained in society and have stable lifestyles (Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2025; Enders et al., 2024), thus having potentially other coping mechanisms.
text.formatted: One potential explanation is that older people are more ingrained in society and have stable lifestyles <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bordeleau & Stockemer, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Enders et al., 2024)</ref>, thus having potentially other coping mechanisms.

text.text: Alternatively, the association may not have manifested because older people have more ingrained thinking styles (either conspiratorial or otherwise) and are thus less likely to change in response to prior distress in comparison to younger people.

It is also possible that many people engage in a conspiratorial mentality for reasons other than compensating for their distress, ranging from simple entertainment (van Prooijen et al., 2022) to rationalising ideological affiliations (Pierre, 2025).

text.text: H2 was supported only regarding anxiety.
In other words, conspiratorial mentality predicts higher anxiety, suggesting that it might be anxiety-provoking for older people.

This can also be hypothetically associated with a greater need to satisfy existential motives (Biddlestone et al., 2025; Douglas et al., 2017), meaning that a conspiratorial mentality might heighten a sense of existential threat, compelling a person to address it.

text.text: This corresponds to the fact that threat is a crucial component of conspiracy theories (Douglas & Sutton, 2018; van Prooijen & Vugt, 2018), and that existential threats are also a relevant covariate of conspiratorial mentality (Biddlestone et al., 2025).

text.text: Given that conspiracy perception tends to exacerbate the perceived threats (van Prooijen, 2020), the results might also suggest a potential vicious cycle between conspiratorial mentality and anxiety.
However, our results did not provide much support for such a cycle, which would require further research with more waves of data.

The role of social media use, hypothesised in H3 and H4, was not supported, suggesting that general social media use is probably not a risk factor regarding conspiratorial mentality among older people.

Given that older people use social media primarily to connect with others (Cotten et al., 2022; Wilson et al., 2021), general social media use encompasses activities unrelated to conspiratorial mentality.
text.formatted: Given that older people use social media primarily to connect with others <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cotten et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wilson et al., 2021)</ref>, general social media use encompasses activities unrelated to conspiratorial mentality.

text.text: Although the role of general social media use was not supported, it is still possible that more specific social media behaviours relate to conspiratorial mentality.

Most notably, using social media to engage with online news may be more relevant, as this behaviour is associated with exposure to false information (Brashier & Schacter, 2020; Grinberg et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Most notably, using social media to engage with online news may be more relevant, as this behaviour is associated with exposure to false information <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brashier & Schacter, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Grinberg et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, it could be helpful for future research to incorporate more nuanced measures of online behaviour that capture a range of social media activities.
Lastly, social media use may also be more closely related to beliefs in specific conspiracy theories than to a more general conspiratorial mentality.
Our main results imply that conspiratorial mentality can be an anxiety-provoking experience.
While anxiety itself is not necessarily pathological, this can have implications for the well-being of older people.
That does not mean that conspiratorial mentality necessarily leads to psychological disorders, as it is usually considered a rather more normative phenomenon.
Nevertheless, strong conspiratorial mentality can still foster anxiety-related experiences or play an important role as a potential cognitive style in fostering potential future psychopathologies.

Given that anxiety is often associated with existential threats (Biddlestone et al., 2025; Douglas et al., 2017; van Prooijen, 2019), these threats may be an important outcome of older people's conspiratorial mentality.

The first limitation is the use of only two waves of data.
This significantly constrained our options for conducting more complex analyses that could yield more precise and robust inferences.
For example, we could not distinguish between-and within-person levels of variance, which is an important feature of the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (Ri-CLPM; Hamaker et al., 2015).

text.text: Still, our research remains well-suited to addressing predictive research questions (Hamaker et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Still, our research remains well-suited to addressing predictive research questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hamaker et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Also, the one-year interval between waves might have influenced our estimates.
Existing literature typically does not provide robust guidance on appropriate time intervals, leaving researchers to make educated guesses (Zhao et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Existing literature typically does not provide robust guidance on appropriate time intervals, leaving researchers to make educated guesses <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Zhao et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, our non-significant results do not necessarily indicate the absence of a psychological mechanism, as some effects might require a different time interval to manifest, and we advise caution when comparing our results with those from other research.
Despite that, we believe our work provides important inferences, as we were interested in capturing more enduring experiences for which longer time intervals are more appropriate (Zhao et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Despite that, we believe our work provides important inferences, as we were interested in capturing more enduring experiences for which longer time intervals are more appropriate <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Zhao et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Another limitation is the use of a one-item measure of social media use, which makes it impossible to assess internal consistency and measurement error, and which also means that this single item can encompass multiple potential activities on social media.

Because of that, our results cannot provide further insight into the different forms of online behaviour that may be associated with conspiratorial mentality, especially those related to news or online information (e.g., Brashier & Schacter, 2020; Grinberg et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Because of that, our results cannot provide further insight into the different forms of online behaviour that may be associated with conspiratorial mentality, especially those related to news or online information (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brashier & Schacter, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Grinberg et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Still, we believe that our results provide important insights into general social media use and underscore the need for a more nuanced approach to online behaviour.
Social desirability bias is also an issue here, as some respondents might have negative associations with the conspiratorial mentality measure.
Some respondents might also underreport their psychological distress due to social desirability.
This might be the case for anxiety and depression, where the distributions were more skewed in comparison to conspiratorial mentality and loneliness.
However, we do not consider this drawback critical, as the data were obtained anonymously, the skewness was not substantial, and the variability of our variables remained sufficient.
Although not exactly a limitation, the issue of distinguishing between general conspiratorial mentality and belief in specific conspiracy theories should also be mentioned.

Although the psychological mechanisms should, in general, operate in the same way in both cases, there is documented heterogeneity in empirical support depending on the measure used (Bowes et al., 2023).

text.text: Thus, it is possible that the effect sizes or statistical significance would differ if we measured beliefs in specific conspiracy theories.
However, as mentioned, we do not consider this a limitation per se, as conspiratorial mentality in general is also relevant and has important implications (Bowes et al., 2023).
